Hi Jordan,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the low latency numbers look promising. Our procurement team has a couple of follow-ups on the hosted rate card before we move toward a PO. Primary question: how do you charge for prompt/prefix caching on the hosted API? Specifically: 

- If a request is served entirely from a cached prefix + cached response (no model execution), do we incur token charges?
- For partial hits (prefix matched but model tails are generated), how are tokens accounted for — do you charge for the whole prompt sent to the model or just the generated suffix?
- Is there any per-request cache-read fee for hosted customers?

We’re trying to baseline costs for budgeting. Can you attach the latest rate card and a short example calculation for a common pattern (20k requests/day, average 40-token prompt, 60-token output, ~25% full cache hit rate)? Procurement is on copy (procurement@midsizeai.com).

Appreciate the quick clarity — aiming to finalize numbers this week.

Hi Susan — great question, and thanks for the clear example workload. I’ve attached our latest rate card and included a short worked example below. Quick TL;DR up front: for hosted API customers, Redwood does not bill model token usage for responses that are satisfied entirely from the prompt/prefix cache (i.e., no model execution). However, there are two important caveats to understand: a small cache-read fee for hosted tiers and how partial hits are metered.

Attachment: redwood_rate_card_v3.pdf (stub)
HubSpot: https://app.hubspot.com/contacts/12345/deal/6789

Detailed behavior: 
1) Full cache hit (response returned without invoking the model):
   - Model token charges: 0 (no model compute used).
   - Hosted cache-read fee: a nominal per-read fee appears on the hosted billing line to cover storage and retrieval costs. On the public rate card the hosted cache-read fee is listed as $0.00009 per cached read; enterprise customers with a committed Dedicated plan can have this rolled into the reserved commit (see enterprise notes on page 2).
   - Data transfer / egress: standard egress pricing applies if responses cross regions.

2) Partial cache hit (prefix matched; suffix generated):
   - We charge tokens for: (a) the portion of the prompt/suffix that is sent to the model runtime (i.e., the non-cached suffix tokens) and (b) all generated output tokens. We do NOT double-charge for the cached prefix tokens.
   - Example: if you have a 40-token prompt where the first 20 tokens are cached and we only need to send the last 20 to the model and then produce 60 tokens of output, you’ll be billed for 20 (input) + 60 (output) = 80 model tokens at the token rate. The cached 20 tokens are not billed as model tokens, but the cache-read fee applies once for that request.

3) Rate card & discounts: baseline hosted token rate is on the attached PDF (see 'Hosted - per token' table). We apply volume discounts to the effective token spend (not to cache-read fees) once you cross the tier thresholds. For large commits / Dedicated reservations we can provide a blended unit price where cache-read fees are included in the monthly commit and further discounts apply.

Worked example (your numbers): 20,000 requests/day, avg 40-token prompt, 60-token output, 25% full cache hit rate.
 - Full hits (25%): 5,000 requests/day -> model tokens = 0; cache-read fees = 5,000 * $0.00009 = $0.45/day
 - Partial/hits (75%): 15,000 requests/day -> assuming average cached prefix = 20 tokens, billed tokens per request = 20 (input) + 60 (output) = 80 tokens -> 1,200,000 tokens/day. At the baseline hosted token rate in the PDF (see page 1) that converts to X/day (refer to attached rate card for per-token $).

Next steps / negotiation: 
If you’d like, I can model exact dollar amounts for the baseline rate and then apply a proposed volume discount for a 12-month commit. For enterprise/Dedicated we can fold cache-read fees into the monthly commitment which simplifies billing and reduces per-read costs to effectively zero for the duration of the commit.

I’ll loop Karthik here for a short technical note on TTL and model-compatibility rules — that affects how often you’ll see full hits vs. partials.

Best,

Hi team — quick technical clarifications to help with the budgeting model: 

- Cache eligibility: a cache entry is keyed by (model, quantization profile, prompt-prefix hash, routing policy). If you change model versions or quantization, that invalidates the entry. So real-world hit rates depend on how stable your prompts + model selection are.
- TTL & size: default hosted prefix cache TTL is 72 hours for non-enterprise tenants. Enterprise customers can request longer TTLs or custom eviction policies as part of Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Partial hit accounting: when we detect a prefix match and we only need to run the model on the remaining suffix we do not re-send the cached prefix to the model runtime; billing and compute are based only on the suffix tokens + generated tokens. This minimizes billed tokens compared to re-sending the whole prompt.
- Edge cases: when we do a cached-response stitch (we return a cached chunk and then re-rank or append a small generated piece) we still bill for the generated tokens plus one cache-read fee.

If you give us a sample of common prompt patterns we can run a small simulation on our side and return an estimated effective cost per 10k requests with your hit assumptions.

Thanks,
Karthik
Principal Product Engineer, Redwood Inference
